technicalFeasibility.rationale: The core stack is mature and off-the-shelf. Bank transaction data is accessible via aggregation APIs (Plaid Transactions product), and transaction categorization is a solved problem where hybrid ML+LLM pipelines reach 85-95% accuracy on known merchants. An LLM adds a natural-language advice/insight layer on top of this proven pipeline. The main non-trivial challenges are cost control (pure-LLM categorization is expensive and slow, so a hybrid rules+ML+LLM design is required), data privacy/compliance handling of financial data, and the well-documented reliability caveat that AI financial advice can produce poor recommendations — not any fundamental technical blocker.
evidence: Plaid offers a Transactions product with per-successful-link pricing ~$0.50-$2.00 and a free tier of ~200 API calls, making bank data access viable for early-stage startups (est. $30K-$65K/yr at ~5K users).
ML-based transaction categorization typically achieves 85-95% accuracy on known merchant categories; a hybrid approach reached 94% accuracy at ~0.2s per transaction.
Industry practice (e.g. ANNA) combines LLMs with traditional ML to cut LLM costs ~75% while keeping accuracy — confirming a cost-effective architecture exists for LLM-in-the-loop finance apps.
Reported risk: over half of Gen Z/millennials who used AI for financial advice said they made a poor decision as a result — a product/safety design constraint, not a feasibility blocker.

marketViability.rationale: Demand signal is strong but the space is crowded and hard to monetize. Students clearly experience financial anxiety and there is measurable appetite for AI-assisted finance (67-77% of Gen Z report using AI for personal finance; budgeting is the top use case at ~60%). However, the student budgeting market is saturated with entrenched incumbents (YNAB with a free student year, PocketGuard, Goodbudget, Rocket Money, Monarch, Copilot, Finny), and Mint's 2024 shutdown showed the 'free-and-everything' model is not sustainable. Students are low-willingness-to-pay, so an 'AI expense tracker for students' risks being a thin feature on top of commodity aggregation unless it has a sharp differentiator. Verdict is medium: real demand exists, but the wedge and monetization path are unproven.
evidence: 67% of Gen Z (up to 77% in one survey) report using AI to help manage personal finances; saving/budgeting is the top AI use case at ~60%.
~73% of Gen Z report feeling anxious about money at least weekly, with students juggling tuition, rent, food, and subscriptions — a clear pain point.
The market is crowded with student-targeted incumbents (YNAB free first year for students, PocketGuard, Goodbudget, Finny free tier, plus general leaders Rocket Money and Monarch).

Mint's March 2024 shutdown left ~3.6M users to migrate and, per market coverage, 'the free-and-everything model died with Mint' — signaling monetization difficulty for a low-willingness-to-pay student segment.
